rationale: The record directly examines access to water and sanitation in informal Roma settlements in Sweden (Criterion 1 & Criterion 4) and focuses on municipal eviction enforcement, informal tenure, and legal/administrative obligations to provide alternative water and sanitation access (Criterion 2 narrow and plain). Although the abstract cites empirical figures ('more than 80 evictions ... between 2013 and 2016') from a multi-university socio-legal report, it does not explicitly describe primary empirical data-collection methods versus doctrinal human rights analysis (Criterion 3 unclear). Per Phase 5 rules against prematurely excluding socio-legal and informal-settlement studies, the record is marked 'unsure' for full-text verification.
plain_vs_narrow_note: No divergence between narrow and plain Criterion 2: municipal eviction/enforcement actions, informal-settlement tenure status, and administrative/legal duties governing alternative water and sanitation provision clearly satisfy both the narrow rule-type reading and the literal plain wording. Full-text retrieval ('unsure') is required under both readings to verify whether the institutional report presents primary socio-legal empirical evidence (Criterion 3) or purely doctrinal legal analysis.

evidence_quotes.quote: Swedish municipalities initiated more than 80 evictions of vulnerable EU citizens, mostly Roma, from informal settlements on the grounds of poor sanitation between 2013 and 2016.
these evictions violated human rights obligations when individuals were offered no alternative access to water and sanitation beyond a few days.
As explained in this report by the Raoul Wallenberg Institute, Sodertorn University and the NuLawLab of Northeastern University School of Law
